planting.note: Direct sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked, or in fall for a cool-season crop in zone 9; Melody, a 1971 All-America Selections winner, is a smooth-leaf spinach bred for good disease resistance and reliable performance.

directions: Direct sow seed a half inch deep in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, thinning seedlings to final spacing. Melody, a 1971 All-America Selections winner, produces smooth to slightly savoyed, dark green leaves with good disease resistance to common spinach ailments, on plants that are somewhat more heat- and bolt-tolerant than many older spinach varieties, useful for extending the harvest a bit later into spring in the Gulf South. Its smooth leaves are easier to clean of grit than heavily crinkled savoy-type spinach. Harvest outer leaves as needed for cut-and-come-again picking, or cut the whole plant at once for a single harvest, and provide light afternoon shade as the weather warms to delay bolting.

common_name: Premium Crop Broccoli (AAS-Winning Classic Hybrid Broccoli)

planting.note: Start seed indoors for a spring crop, or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest; Premium Crop, a 1975 All-America Selections winner, remains a benchmark hybrid broccoli for large, uniform, dense central heads.

directions: Start seed indoors for a spring crop or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, spacing transplants 18 to 24 inches apart. Premium Crop, a 1975 All-America Selections winner, has remained a benchmark hybrid broccoli for decades, prized for exceptionally large, dense, uniform blue-green central heads and reliable heading even under variable growing conditions that can cause other broccoli to head poorly. After the main head is harvested, the plant produces a useful flush of smaller side shoots, extending the harvest for several more weeks. Cut the central head while buds are still tight and before any yellow flowers show, and keep harvesting side shoots as they develop.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Broccoli Production

common_name: Snow Crown Cauliflower (AAS-Winning Early Hybrid Cauliflower)

planting.note: Start seed indoors for a spring crop, or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest; Snow Crown, a 1975 All-America Selections winner, is one of the earliest-maturing cauliflower varieties, forming smooth white heads reliably.

directions: Start seed indoors for a spring crop or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, spacing transplants 18 to 24 inches apart. Snow Crown, a 1975 All-America Selections winner, is one of the fastest-maturing cauliflower varieties available, reliably forming smooth, dense, pure white heads well ahead of many other cultivars, an important advantage in the Gulf South where cauliflower's narrow cool-season window can cut short slower-maturing varieties. Its early maturity also makes it more forgiving of the unpredictable spring warm-ups that can stall cauliflower head formation. Tie or fold outer leaves over the developing head once it is a couple of inches across to blanch it and keep the curds bright white, and harvest promptly once heads reach full size before they begin to separate or discolor.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Cauliflower Production

planting.note: Start seed indoors for a spring crop, or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest; Self Blanche is a classic cauliflower whose leaves naturally curl inward over the developing head, largely eliminating the need to manually tie leaves for blanching.

directions: Start seed indoors for a spring crop or sow in mid to late summer for a fall harvest, spacing transplants 18 to 24 inches apart. Self Blanche is a classic cauliflower variety whose outer leaves naturally curl inward to cover the developing head as it forms, largely eliminating the tedious task of hand-tying leaves over the curd to keep it white, a labor-saving trait especially appreciated by home gardeners growing more than a plant or two. It produces solid, well-formed white heads of good size and quality with this convenient self-blanching habit doing most of the work automatically. Check occasionally to make sure leaves are covering the head adequately, tying loosely if needed, and harvest promptly once heads reach full size before curds begin to separate or yellow.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Cauliflower Production
